summary:
Guadeloupe stands under the national framework of France. The French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply in the territory as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions were subsequently used against LGBTQ people. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure, available since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are not required, and both self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name is handled at the registry office; a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. In 2017 the Court of Cassation rejected a bid to have the law recognise a neutral sex classification.

Conversion therapy was banned in a statute that passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and a fine of up to €30,000. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, a serving member of parliament, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006; the Court of Cassation later cancelled that conviction. Civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders argued that the 2004 statute seriously infringes free speech.

Parental recognition has shifted in the trans-related families case law of the French courts. The Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father; the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised; and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change.

Detention carries documented risk. In French prisons, whose rules apply in Guadeloupe, placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not match gender presentation; in practice, assignment weighs the person's best interests through individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings. The CGLPL, France's oversight body for places of deprivation of liberty, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Guadeloupe has its first LGBT+ centre. The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations, and offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities. The visit of the minister Aurore Bergé for the opening was accompanied by announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted to overseas territories.
tangentialFactors:
Trans minors are a live legislative target in France. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a group opposed to all gender transition for minors to report on youth gender care; it called transition a health scandal and transness a social contagion. A bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 and prompted large-scale protests, with no update recorded since 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Official statements have at times been hostile without altering practice. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an epidemic-like phenomenon and a primarily social problem, advising extreme caution on access; French trans rights organisations reported no change in actual provision. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare, citing lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, and recommended an informed-consent, self-determination model.

Recorded violence against LGBTQ people rose sharply in France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. President Macron had denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France in October 2018 after a rise in attacks. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, sat on the group commissioned to report on youth gender care; one member resigned and the president stepped away.

The historic French regime moved through penalising and then equalising provisions: Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942, later 331, set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982, and the Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity, repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote.

Guadeloupe's community organising is often described against neighbouring jurisdictions: activism on the island is said to be advancing after sister territory Martinique, and three local groups, Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova, partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the French health and education administrations. Gender dysphoria was declassified as a mental illness by decree in 2010, making France the first country to remove gender identity disorder, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under the long-term illness scheme ALD 31 with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979.

Education policy addresses LGBTQ students directly. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008-2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign Tous égaux, tous alliés to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of parent 1 and parent 2 on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage.

Community infrastructure on the island is described as growing. An interview published on 6 September 2023 with Leïla of Guadeloupe's Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, alongside Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's. The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, provides reception, support and orientation locally rather than requiring travel for services.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Senate has voted on the March 2024 compensation bill for men arrested before 1980 is unresolved in the sources, as is any movement on the under-18 transition bill after 23 July 2024.

No source in this inventory reports Guadeloupe-specific enforcement data: there are no figures on prosecutions under the 2004 hate-speech law, the conversion therapy ban or the anti-discrimination statute as applied in the territory, and no territory-level breakdown of the CGLPL's roughly 40 detention referrals since 2010. Whether the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion is resourced on a permanent footing beyond the announced ministerial measures is not sourced.

Entry and visa requirements, customs screening and any territory-specific document checks are not covered by this inventory. The treatment of trans passengers on flights to and from Guadeloupe, and any local practice on identity document presentation at the border, remain not sourced here.
